decks.title: Pollination and Fertilisation — Part 1: Pollination, its agents and the devices that favour crossing
goals: Distinguish self-pollination from cross-pollination and list the advantages and disadvantages of each
Compare insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers and describe the adaptations of water-pollinated flowers
Explain how unisexuality, dichogamy and self-sterility favour cross-pollination

slides.heading: Pollination and Fertilisation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how pollen reaches the stigma, and how plants make sure it comes from another plant.

visual.alt: Flow: anther, pollen grains, agent, stigma

slides.narration: A flower cannot walk to a partner. Yet millions of seeds form every year. The secret is pollination: pollen travels from the anther to the stigma, carried by an agent such as an insect or the wind.

slides.heading: Self-pollination and cross-pollination
slides.body_md: **Pollination** is the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma.

rows: Anther to stigma of the same flower
Anther of one flower to stigma of a flower on another plant of the same kind

visual.alt: Table comparing self-pollination with cross-pollination

slides.narration: In self-pollination, pollen reaches the stigma of its own flower. In cross-pollination, it travels to a flower on a different plant of the same kind. Cross-pollination always needs an outside agent.

slides.heading: Advantages and disadvantages

rows: Sure to happen; needs no agent; little pollen wasted; keeps good traits
New combinations of traits; healthier seedlings; better chance to adapt
Little variation; weaker offspring over many generations
Depends on agents; much pollen wasted; may spread poor traits too

visual.alt: Table of advantages and disadvantages of self-pollination and cross-pollination

slides.narration: Self-pollination is dependable and thrifty, but the offspring all look alike and may weaken over time. Cross-pollination is less certain and wastes pollen, but it brings fresh combinations of traits and stronger, more varied seedlings.

slides.heading: Quick check: bagged flowers
slides.body_md: A flower bud is covered with a bag before it opens and still sets seed. The pollination must have been…
slides.narration: If no agent can reach the flower, which kind of pollination is left?

slides.heading: Agents of pollination

visual.alt: Flow from agents of pollination to insects, wind, water and others

slides.narration: Pollen can be carried by insects such as bees and butterflies, by wind, by water, and sometimes by birds, bats or snails. A flower is shaped by the agent it depends on.

slides.body_md: Look at what each flower **offers** and what it **catches**.

slides.narration: The insect flower has bright scented petals and nectar to attract visitors, and sticky pollen that clings to a body. The wind flower has no petals or nectar. Its anthers hang out to the breeze and its stigma is large and feathery to catch drifting pollen.

slides.heading: Insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers

visual.alt: Table comparing five features of insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers

slides.narration: Compare feature by feature. Insect flowers advertise and reward visitors. Wind flowers do not need to, so they put their effort into making a great deal of light pollen and catching it well.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which agent?
slides.body_md: A plant has small green flowers in a long drooping spike. Anthers hang out on long filaments. The stigmas are feathery. There is no scent and no nectar.
bullets: Step 1: no bright petals, scent or nectar, so insects are **not** being attracted.
Step 2: hanging anthers and a feathery stigma are built to **release and catch** drifting pollen.
Step 3: so the agent is **wind**.

visual.alt: Worked table: clues pointing away from insects and towards wind

slides.narration: Work from the clues. Without bright petals, scent or nectar there is nothing to attract insects. Hanging anthers and feathery stigmas are made for wind. So the plant is wind pollinated.

slides.heading: Quick check: pollen of a wind flower
slides.body_md: Which description fits the pollen of a wind-pollinated flower?
slides.narration: Is it sticky or light? Is there a little or a lot?

slides.narration: In Vallisneria, the male flowers form under water, break off and float up to the surface. The female flower is lifted to the surface on a long coiled stalk. The floating male flowers touch the female flower and pollen is transferred.

slides.heading: How nature favours cross-pollination

rows: Male and female flowers are separate, often on different plants
Anthers and stigma of a flower ripen at different times
Pollen cannot grow on the stigma of the same flower

visual.alt: Table of three devices that favour cross-pollination with an example of each

slides.narration: Plants have three common devices. In unisexual flowers the sexes are separate. In dichogamy, pollen and stigma are ready at different times. In self-sterility, the flower's own pollen simply fails to grow on its own stigma.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a protandrous flower
slides.body_md: In a flower, the anthers shed pollen on days one and two after it opens. The stigma is ready only on days three and four.
bullets: Step 1: pollen is shed **before** the stigma is ready.
Step 2: so the flower's own pollen cannot fertilise it.
Step 3: this is **protandry**, a kind of **dichogamy**; only pollen brought from an older flower can work.

visual.alt: Worked timeline: anthers shed pollen on days one and two, the stigma is ready on days three and four

slides.narration: Read the timeline. The pollen is gone before the stigma is ready. The flower cannot pollinate itself, so it must wait for pollen from another flower. If the stigma ripened first, it would be called protogyny.

slides.heading: Quick check: separate sexes
slides.body_md: True or false: a female papaya flower can be pollinated by its own pollen.
slides.narration: Where must the pollen come from?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Pollination: pollen from anther to stigma.
Self: same flower. Cross: different plants, always needs an agent.
Insect flowers attract; wind flowers make light pollen in huge amounts.
Water: Vallisneria. Devices for crossing: unisexuality, dichogamy, self-sterility.

visual.alt: Summary table of agents and a typical feature of each

slides.narration: To recap. Pollination moves pollen to a stigma. Cross-pollination needs an agent, and flowers show clear adaptations to insects, wind or water. Plants also use separate sexes, different ripening times or self-sterility to favour crossing.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Pollination is **not** fertilisation: one moves pollen, the other fuses gametes.
In comparisons, give a **matching point** for each side.
Name the **example** whenever the question asks for one.
Dichogamy: say **which part ripens first**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Never confuse pollination with fertilisation. In comparisons, give a matching point for each side. Quote an example when asked. And for dichogamy, say which part ripens first.

slides.heading: From Pollen to Seed
slides.body_md: Part 2 — what happens after the pollen lands.

visual.alt: Flow: pollen on stigma, pollen tube grows, fertilisation, fruit and seed

slides.narration: Landing on the stigma is only the beginning. The pollen must grow a tube down to the ovule, deliver its male gametes, and fuse with the female cells. Only then can a seed form.

slides.body_md: A pollen grain on a compatible stigma **germinates**; the **pollen tube** grows down the style to the ovule.

visual.alt: A pistil with pollen grains on the stigma and a pollen tube growing through the style to the ovule

slides.narration: The sugary fluid on the stigma makes the pollen grain germinate. A pollen tube grows out, down the style, through the ovary and into the ovule through its tiny opening, the micropyle. The tube is guided and fed as it grows.

slides.heading: Events from pollination to fertilisation

rows: Pollen grain lands on a suitable stigma and absorbs sugary fluid
It germinates; the tube nucleus leads the pollen tube into the style
The generative nucleus divides, forming two male gametes
The tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and reaches the embryo sac
It bursts and releases the two male gametes

visual.alt: Table of five steps from pollen germination to release of male gametes

slides.narration: Follow the steps. The grain germinates, and the tube nucleus leads the way. The generative nucleus divides into two male gametes. The tube enters the ovule through the micropyle, reaches the embryo sac and releases the gametes.

slides.heading: Quick check: where the tube enters
slides.body_md: The pollen tube enters the ovule through the…
slides.narration: Name the small opening in the ovule.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how long will the tube take?
slides.body_md: A pollen tube grows at a steady 3 millimetres each hour. The style is 15 millimetres long (imagined values).
bullets: Step 1: time = length of style ÷ rate of growth.
Step 3: the tube needs about 5 hours to cross the style.

visual.alt: Worked table: fifteen millimetres at three millimetres an hour takes five hours

slides.narration: Divide the length by the rate. Fifteen divided by three is five. So the tube needs about five hours to cross the style. Real tubes vary in speed, but the method is the same.

slides.heading: Inside the embryo sac
slides.body_md: Egg cell and two **synergids** at the micropyle end; **polar nuclei** in the centre; three **antipodal cells** at the far end.

slides.narration: The embryo sac holds the female cells. The egg cell sits at the micropyle end with two synergids beside it. Two polar nuclei lie in the centre. Three antipodal cells lie at the far end. The pollen tube delivers two male gametes.

slides.heading: Double fertilisation and triple fusion

nodes.label: Male gamete two + two polar nuclei

visual.alt: Flow: one male gamete with the egg cell gives the zygote; the other with two polar nuclei gives the primary endosperm nucleus by triple fusion

slides.narration: Two fusions happen in one embryo sac, which is why it is called double fertilisation. One male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form the zygote. The other fuses with the two polar nuclei. Three nuclei joining is called triple fusion.

slides.heading: Quick check: triple fusion
slides.narration: Which tissue stores food for the embryo?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting chromosomes
slides.body_md: A tomato plant has 24 chromosomes in its body cells.
bullets: Step 1: a gamete has half the number: 24 ÷ 2 = 12.
Step 2: zygote = egg + male gamete = 12 + 12 = 24.
Step 3: endosperm = two polar nuclei + one male gamete = 3 × 12 = 36.

visual.alt: Worked table: gamete twelve, zygote and embryo twenty-four, endosperm thirty-six

slides.narration: Start with the gamete. A tomato gamete has twelve chromosomes, half of twenty-four. The zygote receives twelve from each gamete, so it has twenty-four. The endosperm has three sets of twelve, which is thirty-six.

slides.heading: From flower to fruit and seed

visual.alt: Table of flower parts and what each becomes after fertilisation

slides.narration: After fertilisation the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovule becomes the seed. The zygote grows into the embryo, the endosperm stores food, and the integuments harden into the seed coat. Petals and stamens usually wither.

slides.heading: Quick check: ovary or ovule
slides.body_md: Which part of the flower becomes the fruit?
slides.narration: The fruit is the swollen part that holds the seeds.

slides.heading: Why fruit and seed matter

rows: Holds the embryo and its food store; survives dry or cold periods; grows into a new plant
Protects the seeds; helps spread them by wind, water or animals

visual.alt: Table of the roles of seed and fruit

slides.narration: A seed protects the embryo and supplies food, and can wait until conditions are right. The fruit protects the seeds and helps scatter them, so new plants do not crowd the parent.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Pollen germinates on the stigma; the tube grows to the embryo sac through the micropyle.
One male gamete + egg gives the zygote; the other + two polar nuclei gives the primary endosperm nucleus.
Ovary becomes the fruit; ovule becomes the seed.

visual.alt: Summary table of events and their products

slides.narration: To recap. The pollen tube delivers two male gametes. One forms the zygote with the egg. The other joins the polar nuclei for the endosperm. The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name the **opening** the tube uses: the **micropyle**.
Double fertilisation = **two** fusions; triple fusion is **one of them**.
Show **working** in chromosome counts.
Fruit comes from the **ovary**, seed from the **ovule**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Name the micropyle as the entrance. Remember that triple fusion is one of the two fusions of double fertilisation. Show your working in chromosome counts. And keep ovary and ovule apart.

notes.title: Pollination and Fertilisation — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Self-pollination and cross-pollination
sections.body_md:
**Pollination** is the transfer of **pollen grains** from an **anther** to a **stigma**.

| | Self-pollination | Cross-pollination |
|---|---|---|
| Transfer | Anther to the stigma of the **same flower** (or another flower of the same plant) | Anther of a flower to the stigma of a flower on a **different plant** of the same kind |
| Agent | Often none | Always needed |

**Self-pollination**
- Advantages: sure to happen; needs no agent; little pollen is wasted; good traits are kept.
- Disadvantages: little variation; offspring may become weaker over many generations.

**Cross-pollination**
- Advantages: new combinations of traits; healthier, more varied seedlings; better chance to adapt.
- Disadvantages: depends on agents; much pollen is wasted; poor traits may also spread.

Books differ slightly on pollen moved between two flowers of the same plant; here it is treated as self-pollination (the pollen comes from the same plant).

Pollen reaches the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same kind.

sections.heading: 2. Agents of pollination and flower adaptations
sections.body_md:
Pollen is carried by **insects**, **wind**, **water** and sometimes birds, bats or snails.

| Feature | Insect-pollinated | Wind-pollinated |
|---|---|---|
| Petals | Large, bright, scented | Small, dull or absent |
| Nectar | Present | Absent |
| Pollen | Sticky or spiny; moderate amount | Light, dry, smooth; **huge** amount |
| Stigma | Small and sticky | Large, feathery, often hanging out |
| Anthers | Inside the flower | Hang out on long filaments |

**Water-pollinated flowers** (for example **Vallisneria**): the male flowers form under water, break off and float to the surface; the female flower is carried to the surface on a long, coiled stalk; the floating male flowers touch the female flower and pollen is transferred.

**Diagram:** draw an insect-pollinated and a wind-pollinated flower side by side with their features labelled.

sections.heading: 3. How nature favours cross-pollination
sections.body_md:
| Device | What happens | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Unisexuality** | Male and female flowers are separate, often on different plants | Papaya |
| **Dichogamy** | Anthers and stigma of a bisexual flower ripen at different times | Sunflower (anthers first: **protandry**) |
| **Self-sterility** | Pollen of a flower cannot grow on the stigma of the same flower or plant | Passion fruit |

In **protandry** the anthers ripen first; in **protogyny** the stigma ripens first. Unisexual flowers on **different** plants (dioecious) make self-pollination impossible; flowers of the same plant (monoecious, for example maize) can still be pollinated by pollen from the same plant, so this device is only partly effective.

key_terms.definition_md: Flowers that carry only stamens or only a pistil.
Anthers and stigma of one flower ripen at different times.
A flower's own pollen fails to fertilise it.

sections.heading: 4. From pollination to fertilisation
sections.body_md:
1. A pollen grain lands on a **compatible stigma** and takes up the sugary fluid on it.
2. It **germinates**: a **pollen tube** grows out, led by the **tube nucleus**, down the **style**.
3. The **generative nucleus** divides to form **two male gametes**.
4. The tube enters the **ovule** through the **micropyle** and reaches the **embryo sac**, where it releases the two male gametes.
5. The **embryo sac** holds the **egg cell** with two **synergids** at the micropyle end, two **polar nuclei** in the centre and three **antipodal cells** at the far end.
6. One male gamete fuses with the **egg cell** to form the **zygote** (**fertilisation**).

**Pollination** moves pollen; **fertilisation** is the fusion of male and female gametes. The tube may take several hours to grow through the style; the time varies with the plant.

key_terms.definition_md: A tube that grows from a pollen grain through the style to the ovule.
The small opening in the ovule through which the pollen tube enters.
The female gametophyte inside the ovule; it holds the egg cell and polar nuclei.
The cell formed by fusion of a male gamete and the egg cell.

sections.heading: 5. Double fertilisation, triple fusion, fruit and seed
sections.body_md:
In a flowering plant **two** fusions happen in one embryo sac, so it is called **double fertilisation**:
- male gamete 1 + **egg cell** gives the **zygote** (it grows into the embryo);
- male gamete 2 + **two polar nuclei** gives the **primary endosperm nucleus**. Three nuclei fuse, so this is **triple fusion**; it grows into the **endosperm**, a food store.

**After fertilisation**
| Flower part | Becomes |
|---|---|
| Ovary | Fruit |
| Ovule | Seed |
| Integuments | Seed coat |
| Zygote | Embryo |
| Primary endosperm nucleus | Endosperm |
| Petals, stamens, style, stigma | Usually wither and fall |

**Significance:** the **seed** holds the embryo and its food, survives unfavourable periods and grows into a new plant; the **fruit** protects the seeds and helps to spread them.

Chromosome counts: the gametes are haploid, the zygote is diploid and the endosperm (two polar nuclei plus one male gamete) is triploid. Counts are used only as simple arithmetic here.

key_terms.definition_md: Two fusions in one embryo sac: one forms the zygote, the other the endosperm nucleus.
Fusion of a male gamete with the two polar nuclei.
The food-storing tissue formed from the primary endosperm nucleus.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing **fertilisation** when the question asks for **pollination** (moving pollen is not fusing gametes).
- Giving only one side in a comparison. Give a **matching point** for each side.
- Forgetting that **cross-pollination always needs an agent**.
- Writing triple fusion as a separate event instead of **one of the two fusions** of double fertilisation.
- Mixing up **ovary** (becomes the fruit) and **ovule** (becomes the seed).
- Naming dichogamy without saying **which part ripens first**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, an odd one out **with its category**, a give-reason item.
- 2 marks: two differences or two functions, matched point for point.
- 3 marks: a labelled diagram or three matched points.
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation or diagram with parts of 2 to 4 marks; one part is a labelled diagram.

questions.stem_md: A flower bud is covered with a bag before it opens and still sets seed. The pollination must have been
questions.solution_md: The bag keeps out every agent, so only the flower's own pollen can reach the stigma — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which description fits the pollen of a wind-pollinated flower?

options.text_md: Light, dry and produced in huge amounts
Sticky and produced in small amounts
Sticky and produced in huge amounts

questions.solution_md: Drifting pollen must be light and plentiful, because most grains never reach a stigma — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A female papaya flower can be pollinated by its own pollen.
questions.solution_md: False. A female flower has only a pistil and makes no pollen, so its pollen must come from another flower.

questions.stem_md: The pollen tube enters the ovule through the
questions.solution_md: The tiny opening in the ovule is the micropyle — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Triple fusion produces the
questions.solution_md: A male gamete fuses with two polar nuclei to give the primary endosperm nucleus — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which part of the flower becomes the fruit?
questions.solution_md: The ovary becomes the fruit; the ovules inside it become seeds — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A gardener brushes pollen from the anthers of one rose bush on to the stigmas of a different rose bush. This is
questions.solution_md: Pollen moved to a flower on a different plant of the same kind is cross-pollination — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A farmer prefers a crop that is mostly self-pollinated, because every plant in the field then

options.text_md: keeps the same useful traits as its parent

questions.solution_md: Self-pollination gives offspring very like the parent, so the useful traits are kept — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a disadvantage of cross-pollination?

options.text_md: It depends on an outside agent and wastes much pollen

questions.solution_md: Cross-pollination relies on agents and much pollen is lost — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Self-pollination can take place in a flower that has no insect visitors.

**Reason (R):** Cross-pollination brings new combinations of traits to the seed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the second statement does not explain the first — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Cross-pollination always needs an agent such as insects or wind.
questions.solution_md: True. The pollen has to travel between two different plants, so an agent is needed.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma.

answer.model_answer_md: **Pollination.**

questions.solution_md: Pollination.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: seedlings from cross-pollinated flowers are usually more varied than seedlings from self-pollinated flowers.

answer.model_answer_md: Pollen from a **different plant** brings a **new combination of traits** to the seed.

questions.solution_md: Different parents give new combinations.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between self-pollination and cross-pollination on the basis of where the pollen goes and whether an agent is needed.

answer.model_answer_md: In **self-pollination** pollen reaches the stigma of the **same flower** (or plant) and **often needs no agent**. In **cross-pollination** pollen goes to a flower on a **different plant** of the same kind and an **agent is always needed**.

questions.solution_md: Same flower, no agent; different plant, agent.

marking_scheme.step: Self-pollination: same flower, often no agent

questions.stem_md: State three advantages of cross-pollination over self-pollination.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It brings **new combinations of traits**, so seedlings are more varied.
2. Seedlings are usually **healthier and stronger**.
3. The species has a **better chance to adapt** when conditions change.

questions.solution_md: Variation; vigour; adaptation.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between self-pollination and cross-pollination.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Self-pollination | Cross-pollination |
|---|---|
| Pollen goes to the **same flower** | Pollen goes to a flower on **another plant** |
| **Often needs no agent** | **Always needs an agent** |
| **Little pollen wasted** | **Much pollen wasted** |
| **Little variation** | **More variation** |

questions.solution_md: Destination; agent; wastage; variation.

questions.stem_md: A flower on a drooping spike has no petals, no scent and no nectar. Its anthers swing out on long threads. It is most likely pollinated by
questions.solution_md: Anthers that dangle and no means of attracting insects point to wind — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A flower has large pink petals, a sweet scent and sticky pollen. The sticky pollen is useful because it

options.text_md: clings to the body of a visiting insect

questions.solution_md: Sticky pollen sticks to an insect and is carried to the next flower — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A wind-pollinated flower has a large, feathery stigma. This helps the flower to

options.text_md: catch pollen grains drifting in the air

questions.solution_md: A large feathery surface traps pollen carried by air — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In Vallisneria, pollination takes place when

options.text_md: bees carry pollen under the water
wind blows pollen into the mud
the female flower is pulled under the water
floating male flowers touch the female flower at the water surface

questions.solution_md: Male flowers break off, float up and touch the female flower — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A sage flower makes 2000 pollen grains and a grass flower makes 40000 pollen grains. How many times more pollen does the grass flower make?

**Assertion (A):** A wind-pollinated flower makes a very large amount of pollen.

**Reason (R):** Most of the pollen carried by wind never reaches a stigma.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the loss of most pollen explains why so much is made — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Wind-pollinated flowers usually have large, brightly coloured petals.

**Reason (R):** Wind-pollinated flowers have no need to attract insects.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: wind flowers usually have small, dull petals or none. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The pollen grains of a wind-pollinated flower are usually heavy and sticky.
questions.solution_md: False. They are light, dry and smooth so that the wind can carry them.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the sweet liquid made by many flowers to reward insect visitors.

answer.model_answer_md: **Nectar.**

questions.solution_md: Nectar.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Bright petals, Nectar, Scent, Feathery stigma.

answer.model_answer_md: **Feathery stigma**; the others are **features of insect-pollinated flowers**.

questions.solution_md: The feathery stigma belongs to wind-pollinated flowers.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: a wind-pollinated flower does not make nectar.

answer.model_answer_md: It does not need to **attract insects**, because **wind** carries its pollen.

questions.solution_md: Wind, not insects, is the agent.

questions.stem_md: State two features of the anthers and the stigma of a wind-pollinated flower that help in pollination.

answer.model_answer_md: The **anthers hang out on long filaments**, so the wind can shake the pollen loose. The **stigma is large and feathery**, so it can catch pollen grains drifting in the air.

questions.solution_md: Hanging anthers; feathery stigma.

marking_scheme.step: Anthers hang out on long filaments

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which an insect-pollinated flower attracts visiting insects.

answer.model_answer_md: Its **petals are large, bright and scented**, and it makes **nectar** as a reward for the visitor.

questions.solution_md: Bright scented petals; nectar.

questions.stem_md: Describe how pollination is brought about in Vallisneria.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **male flowers** form **under water**, break off and **float** to the surface.
2. The **female flower** is carried to the surface by a **long, coiled stalk**.
3. The floating male flowers **touch the female flower** and pollen is **transferred to the stigma**.

questions.solution_md: Male flowers float; female on coiled stalk; contact.

marking_scheme.step: Male flowers break off and float
Female flower reaches the surface on a coiled stalk

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between an insect-pollinated flower and a wind-pollinated flower.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Insect-pollinated | Wind-pollinated |
|---|---|
| **Large, bright, scented** petals | Petals **small, dull or absent** |
| **Nectar** present | **No nectar** |
| Pollen **sticky**, moderate amount | Pollen **light and dry**, huge amount |
| Stigma **small and sticky** | Stigma **large and feathery** |

questions.solution_md: Petals; nectar; pollen; stigma.

questions.stem_md: Some papaya trees in an orchard bear flowers with only stamens; others bear flowers with only a pistil and are the only ones that fruit. Fruit forms only after pollen arrives from the first group because these flowers are
questions.solution_md: Male and female flowers on different plants force cross-pollination — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a bisexual flower the stigma becomes receptive several days after the anthers have shed their pollen. This condition is
questions.solution_md: Anthers ripening first is protandry — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Pollen from a flower is placed on its own stigma but no pollen tube grows. This device that favours cross-pollination is
questions.solution_md: Pollen that cannot grow on its own stigma shows self-sterility — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Dichogamy helps to prevent self-pollination in a bisexual flower.

**Reason (R):** In dichogamy the anthers and the stigma of the flower ripen at different times.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true; ripening at different times is how dichogamy prevents self-pollination — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In papaya, cross-pollination is the only way to set fruit.

**Reason (R):** Papaya plants have bisexual flowers.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true, because the sexes are on different plants. The reason is false: papaya flowers are unisexual — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the condition in which the anthers and the stigma of the same flower ripen at different times.

answer.model_answer_md: **Dichogamy.**

questions.solution_md: Dichogamy.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Unisexuality, Dichogamy, Self-sterility, Nectar.

answer.model_answer_md: **Nectar**; the others are **devices that favour cross-pollination**.

questions.solution_md: Nectar attracts insects; it is not a device that prevents self-pollination.

questions.stem_md: In a flower the stigma is receptive on days 1 and 2 after it opens, and the anthers shed pollen on days 4 and 5. How many whole days lie between the last receptive day of the stigma and the first pollen day?
questions.solution_md: The stigma is last receptive on day 2 and pollen is first shed on day 4, so the empty days are those between them: $4 - 2 - 1 = 1$ (day 3).

questions.stem_md: Name two devices by which nature favours cross-pollination and give an example of one of them.

answer.model_answer_md: **Unisexuality** (separate male and female flowers, for example **papaya**), **dichogamy** (anthers and stigma ripen at different times) or **self-sterility** (own pollen cannot grow on the stigma). Any two with one example.

questions.solution_md: Any two devices with an example.

questions.stem_md: Explain how dichogamy favours cross-pollination. Name the two kinds of dichogamy and state which part ripens first in each.

answer.model_answer_md: When the anthers and the stigma of a flower ripen at **different times**, the pollen of the flower is **not ready when its own stigma is receptive**, so pollen must come from **another flower**. In **protandry** the **anthers ripen first**; in **protogyny** the **stigma ripens first**.

questions.solution_md: Different times prevent self-pollination; protandry anthers first; protogyny stigma first.

questions.stem_md: Why does unisexuality favour cross-pollination? Name one plant that shows it with male and female flowers on different plants.

answer.model_answer_md: Male and female flowers on **different plants** mean that pollen has to be carried from one plant to another, which is **cross-pollination**. Example: **papaya**.

questions.solution_md: Separate plants force crossing; papaya.

questions.stem_md: A pollen grain placed on a suitable stigma takes up sugary fluid and then produces a thread-like outgrowth. This outgrowth is the
questions.solution_md: The germinating pollen grain produces the pollen tube — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a growing pollen tube, the generative nucleus divides to form
questions.solution_md: The generative nucleus gives two male gametes — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the figure of a pistil after pollination, which letter marks the small opening through which the pollen tube enters the ovule?
questions.solution_md: F is the micropyle; A is the stigma, B the pollen tube, C the style, D the ovary wall and E the ovule — option (a).

questions.stem_md: State what each of the following becomes after fertilisation: (i) ovary, (ii) ovule.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The **ovary** becomes the **fruit**, which protects the seeds. (ii) The **ovule** becomes the **seed**, which holds the embryo and its stored food.

questions.solution_md: Ovary to fruit; ovule to seed.

questions.stem_md: Explain double fertilisation. State what is formed by each fusion.

answer.model_answer_md: Two male gametes are released in the embryo sac and **two fusions** take place. **One male gamete fuses with the egg cell** to form the **zygote**. **The other fuses with the two polar nuclei** (**triple fusion**) to form the **primary endosperm nucleus**.

questions.solution_md: Two fusions; zygote; primary endosperm nucleus.

questions.stem_md: State the significance of (i) a seed and (ii) a fruit to a plant.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The **seed** holds the **embryo with its food store**, can **survive dry or cold periods** and **grows into a new plant**. (ii) The **fruit protects the seeds** and **helps to spread them** by wind, water or animals.

questions.solution_md: Seed: embryo, food, survival; fruit: protection, spread.

marking_scheme.step: Seed survives bad periods and grows

questions.stem_md:
A student studies tomato flowers. She uses 40 buds in each of four sets. Set P: buds bagged with anthers left in place. Set Q: anthers removed, stigmas dusted with pollen from another plant, then bagged. Set R: anthers removed and bagged, no pollen added. Set S: buds left open. The number of buds that formed fruit was P 34, Q 38, R 0, S 36.

(a) Which set shows self-pollination and which shows cross-pollination? [2]

(b) Calculate the percentage of buds that formed fruit in sets P and S. [2]

(c) Explain why no fruit formed in set R. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of an insect-pollinated flower, labelling four features that attract insects or catch pollen. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **P** shows self-pollination (own pollen, no other pollen can enter the bag). **Q** shows cross-pollination (pollen from another plant).

**(b)** P: 34 ÷ 40 × 100 = **85%**. S: 36 ÷ 40 × 100 = **90%**.

**(c)** The anthers were removed and the bag kept out every agent, so **no pollen reached the stigma**; without pollination there is **no fertilisation and no fruit**.

**(d)** A flower with **large bright scented petals**, **nectar**, a **sticky stigma** and **sticky pollen on anthers inside**; four labels with ruled lines.

questions.solution_md: P self; Q cross; 85% and 90%; no pollen reached the stigma; labelled insect flower.

marking_scheme.step: No pollination, so no fertilisation or fruit
Flower drawn with petals, stigma and anthers

questions.stem_md:
Pollen grains of one plant are placed in sugar solutions of different strength and 200 grains are counted on each slide after some hours. Grains that germinated: 0 percent sugar 14; 5 percent 62; 10 percent 118; 15 percent 90; 20 percent 34.

(a) Calculate the percentage of grains that germinated in the 0 percent and the 10 percent solutions. [2]

(b) Which solution was best for germination? What does this suggest about the fluid on a stigma? [2]

(c) State what is formed when a pollen grain germinates, and why germinated grains are needed for fertilisation. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a pistil showing a pollen tube growing from the stigma to the ovule, with four labels. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 0 percent: 14 ÷ 200 × 100 = **7%**. 10 percent: 118 ÷ 200 × 100 = **59%**.

**(b)** The **10 percent solution**. The result suggests that the **sugary fluid on a stigma** helps pollen grains to germinate.

**(c)** A **pollen tube** is formed. The tube carries the **male gametes** down the style to the ovule, so a grain that does not germinate cannot fertilise.

**(d)** A **stigma** at the top, a **style**, a swollen **ovary** with an **ovule** and the **micropyle**; the **pollen tube** drawn as a line from the stigma through the style into the micropyle. Four labels.

questions.solution_md: 7% and 59%; 10 percent best, stigma fluid helps; pollen tube carries male gametes; labelled pistil.

marking_scheme.step: Carries male gametes to the ovule
Pistil with tube from stigma to micropyle

questions.stem_md:
A botanist compares two plants. A sage flower makes 2000 pollen grains and and is visited by bees. A grass flower makes 40000 pollen grains; its anthers hang out of the flower and it has a single ovule.

(a) Name the likely pollinating agent of each plant. [2]

(b) Calculate how many times more pollen the grass flower makes, and give one reason for the difference. [3]

(c) State two other features that adapt the grass flower to its agent. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a wind-pollinated flower, labelling three features. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Sage: **insects (bees)**. Grass: **wind**.

**(b)** 40000 ÷ 2000 = **20 times**. Wind carries pollen at random, so **most grains are wasted** and a huge amount must be made.

**(c)** A **large feathery stigma** to catch pollen, and **light, dry pollen** that the wind can carry (or no petals or nectar).

**(d)** A **stem** carrying a **feathery stigma**, **anthers hanging out on long filaments** and **small or no petals**; three labels.

questions.solution_md: Sage insects, grass wind; 20 times, much wasted; feathery stigma and light pollen; labelled wind flower.

marking_scheme.step: Reason linked to the number of grains

questions.stem_md:
A student keeps Vallisneria in a glass tank. She sees small flowers floating on the water surface and a few other flowers on long coiled stalks that reach the surface.

(a) Name the agent of pollination in this plant. [1]

(b) State what the floating flowers are and what happens to them before they float. [2]

(c) Explain the use of the long coiled stalk of the other flowers. [2]

(d) State what happens when the floating flowers touch the flowers on the long stalks. [1]

(e) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of pollination in Vallisneria, labelling four parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Water**.

**(b)** They are the **male flowers**. They **form under water and break off**, then rise and float.

**(c)** The coiled stalk **carries the female flower up to the water surface**, where the floating male flowers can reach it (and it can stretch or coil as the water level changes).

**(d)** **Pollen is transferred from the male flowers to the stigma** of the female flower.

**(e)** The **water surface**, a **male flower floating**, a **female flower on a long coiled stalk**, and the **plant under water**. Four labels.

questions.solution_md: Water; floating male flowers; coiled stalk raises the female flower; pollen transferred; labelled diagram.

marking_scheme.step: Stalk lifts the female flower to the surface
Surface, male and female flowers drawn

questions.stem_md:
A fruit of a plant contains 40 seeds. In each seed an embryo and its endosperm formed after one pollen tube delivered two male gametes to one embryo sac. The plant has 24 chromosomes in each body cell.

(a) How many pollen tubes and how many male gametes were used to form the 40 seeds? [2]

(b) Name the two fusions that take place in each embryo sac and state what each produces. [3]

(c) How many chromosomes does the zygote have? [1]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of an embryo sac, labelling five parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** One tube for each seed: **40 pollen tubes**; two male gametes for each: 40 × 2 = **80 male gametes**.

**(b)** **Male gamete + egg cell** gives the **zygote** (fertilisation). **Male gamete + two polar nuclei** gives the **primary endosperm nucleus** (triple fusion).

**(c)** Each gamete has 24 ÷ 2 = 12; the zygote has 12 + 12 = **24**.

**(d)** An oval **embryo sac** with **egg cell**, two **synergids** near the micropyle, two **polar nuclei** in the centre and three **antipodal cells** at the far end. Five labels.

questions.solution_md: 40 tubes and 80 gametes; zygote and primary endosperm nucleus; 24 chromosomes; labelled embryo sac.

questions.stem_md:
Study the diagram of an embryo sac at the time of fertilisation. Parts are lettered A to E.

(a) Name the parts B and C. [2]

(b) State what the part E is and how it reached the embryo sac. [2]

(c) State what happens when E meets B and when E meets C. [3]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a flower after fertilisation, showing what the ovary and the ovule become. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** B is the **egg cell**; C is the pair of **polar nuclei**.

**(b)** E is a **male gamete**. It was carried by the **pollen tube**, which entered the ovule through the **micropyle**.

**(c)** E + B: fertilisation, forming the **zygote**. E + C: **triple fusion**, forming the **primary endosperm nucleus**.

**(d)** A fruit in section showing the **fruit wall** (from the ovary), the **seed** (from the ovule) with its **seed coat**, **embryo** and **endosperm**. Labels.

questions.solution_md: Egg cell, polar nuclei; male gamete via pollen tube; zygote and primary endosperm nucleus; labelled fruit.
